errors_in_other_reviews: gpt, claim 1, verdict rests on a non-authoritative metadata page. gpt returned Not established because 'the API metadata available during review listed the base dataset's last update as 2026-07-22', citing https://dev.socrata.com/foundry/data.edmonton.ca/tq23-qn4m. That is Socrata's developer documentation page for the dataset, not the dataset's own metadata. The Socrata metadata for tq23-qn4m records rowsUpdatedAt of 2026-09-03, and two reviewers working independently queried records through 2026-07-31T23:45 and returned the identical figure of 1,291,714. Coverage of the required window is established, not unverified, and the brief's short-window rule was never triggered.

gpt, claim 1, verdict-bearing weight placed on a media report. gpt's only supporting item is the CBC analysis republished by Yahoo. The brief says a news report is a lead to the source behind it and never the source of a verdict figure. gpt was right not to let it carry Supported, but that leaves its claim 1 position resting entirely on a documentation page's stale timestamp, with no primary extract on either side.

gpt, claim 2, treats a reviewer's inability to compute as a property of the record. The brief's Not established conditions for claim 2 are exhaustive and specific: an empty verdict set, an unclassifiable counter that passed tests 1 and 2, or an under-reported counter in the set. gpt reports none of these obtained; it reports that it could not execute the spatial join from the interfaces available to it. Two reviewers executed it and returned the same 20-counter set with medians agreeing counter by counter. 'I could not reproduce it' and 'the published record does not permit it' are different findings and the ladder only responds to the second.

gpt, claims 6 and 7, wrong denominator in the work-at-home alternative. gpt computes 102,215 divided by (102,215 plus 380,315) equals 21.2 percent, and a car share of 323,705 divided by 482,530 equals 67.1 percent. The census place of work status universe for Edmonton in 2021 is 483,855, not 482,530: about 1,330 people worked outside Canada and are in the universe but in neither of gpt's two categories. Using the published universe gives a work-at-home share of 21.12 percent and a car share of 66.9 percent. The error is small and does not move any verdict, but this brief exists because figures are being quoted without their denominators, so a constructed denominator that drops a category should not stand.

gemini, claim 3, a citation that cannot say what is claimed of it. gemini attributes to 'Bicycle ridership and intention in a northern, low-cycling city' (Travel Behaviour and Society, published 2018-08-01) a finding that the circulating 1 to 2 percent figure 'is derived from Journey to Work census commuting data (0.88%) or travel survey mode share (1.7%)'. The 0.88 percent figure is the 2021 Census bicycle commuting share, released 2022-11-30, more than four years after that paper was published. A 2018 paper cannot contain it. Whatever the paper says, it does not say this.

gemini, claim 3, a source URL that points at the wrong dataset. gemini's challenging item titled '2014 Bike Ridership Mixed Topic Survey', publisher City of Edmonton, dated 2014-08-25, carries the URL https://data.edmonton.ca/resource/tq23-qn4m.json. That is the Eco-Counter bicycle and pedestrian counts endpoint. The bike ridership survey is dataset nhbh-yj57. A reader following the citation reaches counter passages, not survey responses.

gemini, claim 3, a survey figure that does not match the dataset. gemini reports that '62% of respondents reported riding a bicycle at least once a year' in the 2014 survey. The published dataset records 40.1 percent of 816 respondents choosing 'Never ride a bike', so 59.9 percent chose a riding frequency, and gpt's read of the peer-reviewed analysis of the same panel gives 57.6 percent. The 62 percent figure matches neither. It carries no verdict in gemini's answer, but it is a number that would be quoted.

gemini, claim 3, a numerator mismatch presented as support. gemini files the mode-share item as supporting evidence for a population participation ceiling. Mode share of commuting journeys and share of residents who ride at all are different numerators over different denominators. The brief's central instruction is that a measure of one thing may not be set against a claim about another. gemini's own establishes line concedes the point, which makes the filing the error rather than the reading.

gemini, claim 2, a sum of two medians reported as a corridor median. gemini reports that '132 Avenue carried a combined median of 150.0 bikes/day across two counters (132 Ave E of 108 St N: 71.0; 132 Ave E of 108 St S: 79.0)'. Seventy-one plus seventy-nine is a sum, not a median, and the brief fixes the measure as the median daily count at each counter, each reported individually. The two counters sit at the same location on opposite sides, so the sum also counts a rider passing both twice. The correct report is 71 and 79, each on its own, and both are above the primary cutoff, so the verdict does not turn on it.

gemini, claim 2, an off-street counter used to refute a named corridor without saying it is outside the verdict set. gemini's evidence that named lanes are busy lists Hermitage North at 148 bicycles per day alongside the four in-set corridors, under an establishes line reading 'Refutes the claim of little or no use on the specific named corridors'. No Hermitage counter appears in the 20-counter set gemini itself derived, so it was excluded at test 3 or test 4. The brief requires that such a counter's figures be given with the reason it is outside the set stated. Presenting it in the same breath as in-set counters reads as though the metered-lane finding covers Hermitage. It does not.

gemini, claim 2, an explanation of perception offered where the brief forbids testing perception. gemini's limitations say the motor vehicle volumes explain 'why 100 to 1,000 bicycles spread over 16 daylight hours visually appear sparse to passing drivers'. The brief states the claim is not tested as a claim about what anyone saw, because nothing in the public record can establish what a person driving past noticed. Reporting the vehicle counts is required; asserting what they cause a driver to perceive is a claim the record cannot carry, in either direction.

gemini, claim 2, an overstated unmetered denominator. gemini's limitations say the counters 'monitor approximately 20 points along 384.72 km of active on-road routes'. The ON ROAD total in the Bike Routes dataset includes signed routes and shared on-road facilities. On-street bike lane proper, that is protected plus painted plus contra-flow, is about 90.8 km by my measurement of the same geometry. Setting 20 counters against 384.72 km overstates how much bike lane went unmeasured. The direction of the error cuts against gemini's own verdict, which is why it is worth naming rather than letting stand.

gemini, claim 7, a regional figure leading the reasoning on a City proposition. gemini's interpretation notes and its first supporting item lead with the Edmonton census metropolitan area share of 87.40 percent, 'rounding directly to the stated 87%', and describe both City and CMA as falling in the Supported band. The brief fixes the City of Edmonton census subdivision as the primary geography and says a CMA figure is a required alternative reported under its own name and never called a City figure. The verdict is the same either way, because the City's 85.11 percent is inside the band on its own, but the reasoning as written lets the region carry the city's claim.

gemini, claim 7, an arithmetic slip in the work-at-home alternative. gemini reports that including people working at home drops the car share to about 66.1 percent. The figure is 66.9 percent on the published place-of-work universe of 483,855, 67.1 percent on gpt's constructed 482,530, and 67.4 percent on gemini's own stated inputs of 380,320 plus about 100,000. No available denominator produces 66.1 percent.

gemini, claim 8, the published purpose-by-mode table was missed. gemini returns Not established on the ground that the 2015 summary reports do 'not publish a cross-tabulation of bicycle trips specifically broken down by purpose'. The summary report's purpose table gives trip totals for every purpose with the bicycle share within each purpose, which is a published breakdown of bicycle trips by purpose at rounded precision. Both other reviewers used it and returned figures within a point of each other. The brief expressly permits a reviewer to compute a share the source does not print, provided the arithmetic is shown and labelled. This is the one substantive verdict disagreement on the panel and I do not think gemini's is right.

gemini, claim 8, path location offered as a proxy for trip purpose. gemini files 'river valley and shared-use paths carry roughly half of all recorded bicycle counts' as supporting evidence 'demonstrating heavy recreational corridor usage'. The High Level Bridge, the single busiest counter in the network, is a shared path and a commuting spine. Where a rider is does not establish why they are riding, and gemini's own establishes line says so, which again makes the filing the error.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Edmonton's automated counters recorded nearly 1.3 million cycling trips in the first seven months of 2026.
claims.interpretation_notes: Unchanged from round 1: Supported, High confidence. The sum of total_cyclist_count in tq23-qn4m for log_timestamp from 2026-01-01T00:00:00 to 2026-07-31T23:45:00 is 1,291,714, which sits inside the primary Supported band of at least 1.10 million and below 1.50 million and inside the alternative band of at least 1.17 million and below 1.43 million. The verdict is not definition-sensitive. gemini queried the same endpoint independently and returned the identical figure to the unit, which is the strongest form of confirmation available here. gpt returned Not established on the ground that it could not verify the dataset covered the full window, citing a developer documentation page listing a last update of 2026-07-22. That page is not the dataset's metadata. The Socrata metadata for tq23-qn4m gives rowsUpdatedAt of 2026-09-03, and the extract runs to 2026-07-31T23:45 across 933,576 fifteen-minute records. The brief's short-window rule was written for the case where the published record stops before 2026-07-31, and that case did not arise. I hold Supported. The City calls these counts, not trips, and I use the City's word: the figure is 1,291,714 counted passages, over no denominator, and it is not a count of people or of journeys.

supporting_evidence.finding: Sum of total_cyclist_count for log_timestamp from 2026-01-01T00:00:00 to 2026-07-31T23:45:00 = 1,291,714, over 933,576 fifteen-minute records at 48 distinct counter locations. Query run 2026-09-03 against the Socrata endpoint https://data.edmonton.ca/resource/tq23-qn4m.json with $select=sum(total_cyclist_count) and the date range in $where. 41 of the 48 locations recorded a non-zero cyclist count; the other 7 are pedestrian-configured. gemini ran the same aggregation independently and returned 1,291,714.

limitations: A counter records a passage past a fixed point. It is not a person and it is not a journey. One person riding to work and home past the same counter is two counts, one journey past two counters is two counts, and a person riding where there is no counter is none. The City labels the field total_cyclist_count.
The figure has no denominator. It is a raw count and the story should print it as one.

Roughly half the network total comes from river valley and shared-use path counters and roughly half from on-street counters, so this total is not a measure of bike-lane use. gemini's split of the 2026 window is 646,365 counts at 20 on-street counters and 645,349 at 28 off-street counters.

The City's own data description warns the records are raw and unaudited. The CBC article reports the City acknowledging that pedestrian and cyclist counts were switched at three sites, affecting 2021 and 2022, which is outside this window but shows the class of error the raw data can contain.

This claim and bike-lanes-look-empty both come out of tq23-qn4m. This claim takes a network total over seven months of 2026; that claim takes per-counter daily medians for July 2025 at on-street counters only. A large network total establishes nothing about any one corridor.

claims.proposition_evaluated: The Edmonton bike lanes that are metered, including the lanes residents named as empty, carry little or no bicycle traffic.
claims.interpretation_notes: Unchanged from round 1: Contradicted under the primary cutoff, High confidence, and definition-sensitive. Applying the brief's five tests I reached a verdict set of 20 on-street counters, all in service through July 2025 and all reporting the full month, with July 2025 median daily bicycle counts from 46 to 979. No counter is below the primary cutoff of 25 a day, so no counter is below it and the ladder returns Contradicted. Under the alternative cutoff of 50, one counter, 96 Street S of Jasper Ave at 46, falls below and nineteen do not, so the alternative returns Partially supported. The story cannot fairly quote this verdict without that. gemini reached the same 20-counter set and the same medians working independently, including the same single out-of-service removal at 106 Street N of Jasper Avenue, which is the strongest available check on a membership rule this intricate. gpt returned Not established because it could not execute the spatial join. I do not follow it there: the brief's Not established conditions for this claim are an empty set, an unclassifiable counter, or an under-reported counter, and none of the three obtained. A reviewer's inability to compute a figure is not a finding about the published record. Two features of the data survive the verdict and belong beside it. The corridors residents named are genuinely at the quiet end of the metered set, 71 and 79 on 132 Avenue and 152 on 119 Avenue against 979 on 83 Avenue, an order of magnitude apart. And no counter sits on Whyte Avenue itself.

supporting_evidence.finding: The lowest July 2025 median in the verdict set, 96 Street S of Jasper Ave at 46 bicycles/day, is the only counter that falls below the alternative cutoff of 50. It is also the only one that could be described as quiet relative to the rest: its 2025 calendar-year total is 8,661 against 200,981 at 83 Avenue W of 99 Street. Under the alternative cutoff the verdict would be Partially supported rather than Contradicted, which is the one respect in which the holders' statement survives contact with the meters.

The City publishes no measure of what share of its lane kilometres are metered, and a counter is a point rather than a length, so no share can honestly be computed. Setting 20 counters against the whole 384.4 km ON ROAD figure would overstate the unmeasured remainder, because that figure includes signed and shared on-road routes that are not bike lanes.

claims.interpretation_notes: Unchanged from round 1: Contradicted, Moderate confidence. This is the one claim where the panel splits, and I hold my position against gemini's Not established. gemini returns Not established on the ground that the 2015 survey does not publish a bicycle-by-purpose cross-tabulation. It does publish one, at rounded precision: the summary report's purpose table gives trip totals for every purpose with the bicycle share within each, and the brief expressly permits a reviewer to compute a share the source does not print provided the arithmetic is shown and labelled. gpt and I used that table independently and landed within a point of each other. On the survey's own categories, recreational bicycle trips (HB-Social/Rec) are about 11,994, and work-related bicycle trips (HB-Work plus NHB-Work) about 21,379, of which HB-Work alone is about 19,521 and is the largest single purpose. Recreation is 21.2 percent of my derived bicycle total of about 56,605 and 21.9 percent of the survey's published 54,800, and either way it is far below 35 percent while work exceeds it. The ladder returns Contradicted on two independent grounds, and the same under the alternative cutoffs. I tested the rounding, which is the real weakness here: taking every rounded whole-percent cell across its full interval, recreation ranges from 18.2 to 25.5 percent of bicycle trips and work from 31.4 to 46.6 percent, so recreation stays below 35 percent and below work across the entire range. The verdict is robust to the rounding. I keep confidence at Moderate rather than High because the shares are reviewer arithmetic on rounded cells and because HB-Social/Rec bundles social visits with recreation, though that bundling can only inflate the recreational share, which still fails. The counter shape, which points the same way, is context and carries nothing.

supporting_evidence.finding: Two Edmonton sources point the other way and are worth stating because they are what a holder of this claim would reach for. The City's August 2014 bike ridership survey asked riders why they ride, multi-select: of 482 respondents who answered, 87.3 percent ticked recreation or leisure enjoyment, 47.5 percent transportation trips, 42.1 percent commuting to work or school and 19.9 percent other reasons. This is an opt-in panel, the answers are reasons rather than trips, and the percentages sum well past 100 because people ticked more than one, so it cannot carry the verdict. But it does show most riders in that sample ride for recreation at least sometimes, which is a different proposition from most cycling being recreational.
